source.version: Journal version of record, Frontiers in Psychology 16:1636906, published 08 September 2025; DOI 10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1636906 (p. 1).
source.title_on_document: Why unequal AI access enhances team productivity: the mediating role of interaction processes and cognitive diversity

supplement.holds: According to the main PDF: Section 1 contains writing-task instructions (p. 6, Section 3.3); Section 2 contains evaluation instructions and examples of high- and low-scoring submissions (pp. 6-7, Section 3.4.2.1); Section 3 contains the Interaction Process Analysis coding framework (p. 7, Section 3.4.4). No additional statistics or standard-error tables in the supplement can be confirmed. The supplement was not available locally, and attempts to access the stated publisher URL and the DOI URL with urllib were blocked by network permissions.

paper_design_summary: In a laboratory experiment, 120 Chinese university students formed 60 two-person teams and first wrote a press release without AI. Teams were then randomly assigned to unequal Kimi access (one member) or full access (both members) for a second press release; the no-AI phase always preceded the AI phase and used a different product prompt (pp. 5-7, Sections 3-3.3 and Figure 3). Marketing professionals graded the writing, and an embedding measure compared the two teammates’ spoken contributions (pp. 6-7, Sections 3.4.2.1 and 3.4.3).

studies.label: Laboratory team press-release experiment: unequal versus full AI access, with a common no-AI baseline

assignment.what_was_assigned: Students were randomly formed into two-person teams. Teams were randomly assigned to unequal versus full AI access for the treatment-phase task; within unequal-access teams, the member permitted to use AI was also randomly selected. The no-AI task was a common first phase, not a third randomized arm, and condition order was not randomized (pp. 5-6, Sections 3 and 3.2; p. 7, Figure 3).
assignment.quote: Then, in the treatment phase, these teams were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: only one member could use GenAI (unequal access), or both members could use it (full access).
assignment.locator: p. 6, Section 3 Method, opening paragraph; Section 3.2; p. 7, Figure 3.

arms.name: Unequal AI access
arms.description: Treatment-phase press release with only one randomly selected member of each two-person team permitted to use Kimi; the partner could not directly use it (p. 6, Sections 3 and 3.2). Table 3 reports Condition 1 N = 40 teams (p. 11). Arm-specific people counts at assignment or analysis are not explicitly printed, so these numeric fields are null rather than copying the team count.

arms.name: Full AI access
arms.description: Treatment-phase press release with both members permitted to use Kimi (p. 6, Sections 3 and 3.2). Table 3 reports Condition 2 N = 20 teams (p. 11). Arm-specific people counts at assignment or analysis are not explicitly printed, so these numeric fields are null rather than copying the team count.

arms.name: No AI access (earlier common baseline)
arms.description: All teams first completed a press release without GenAI. This is the same participants in an earlier task, not an independent randomized control arm; its people count must not be added to the treatment-phase sample (p. 6, Sections 3-3.3; p. 7, Figure 3).

participants.exclusions: No exclusions or attrition are reported. The stated experimental sample is 120 people in 60 two-person teams (pp. 5-6, Sections 3 and 3.1); the analyzed team groups in Table 3 are N = 40 and N = 20 (p. 11). The nine marketing raters and the 120 writing submissions are not additional experimental participants (p. 7, Section 3.4.2.1).
participants.who: Undergraduate and graduate students from various majors at a university in China, collaborating face to face in two-person teams (pp. 5-6, Sections 3 and 3.1).
participants.quote: This experiment involved 120 participants, who were made up of undergraduates and graduate students from a university in China.
participants.locator: pp. 5-6, Section 3 Method (recruitment and random assignment of the stated sample); p. 6, Section 3.1 Participants; p. 11, Table 3 (team counts in analysis).

ai_tool.name_model: Kimi 3.0, developed by Moonshot, as named by the document (p. 6, Sections 3 and 3.2).
ai_tool.how_used: Authorized team members received a link to Kimi with no restriction on how to interact with it. Everyone had task instructions and basic document-editing tools; other websites and applications were prohibited unless instructed. On-site recordings were reviewed for compliance (p. 6, Section 3.2).

task.description: Teams collaboratively wrote a 700-character Chinese press release about an electric bicycle in the no-AI phase and AR glasses in the AI phase. Basic product information and writing instructions were supplied. The different prompts and fixed order are acknowledged limitations (p. 6, Sections 3.2-3.3; p. 14, Section 5.4).
task.duration: Each writing task was limited to 45 minutes (p. 6, Section 3.3).

outcomes.name: Task quality: overall expert grade, with originality-only robustness measure
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Blinded marketing professionals assigned an overall grade from 1 to 7 based on writing quality, content quality, and originality. Nine professionals evaluated the 120 submissions, with three raters per submission and 40 submissions per rater; Cronbach alpha = 0.791 (pp. 6-7, Section 3.4.2.1). Coded as usefulness because the main measure is an overall task-quality grade, not an explicitly named overall-creativity rating. In Section 4.4.2, originality is used as the sole indicator of task quality in a robustness mediation model; it is retained here as a novelty-focused variant of the same outcome under form rule 7 (pp. 10-11; p. 12, Figure 6). Writing quality and content quality have no separately reported outcome results. The main OLS analysis reports N = 120 submission observations (p. 9, Table 1); this is not a count of independent teams. The originality mediation model instead reports N = 60 (p. 11).

contrasts.reported: Task quality: unequal access M = 5.654, SD = 0.080; full access M = 5.250, SD = 0.118; t = 2.881, p < 0.01 (p. 8, Section 4.1). Table 1, Model (1), prints Full access to AI b = −0.4023**, adjacent column headed SD = −2.2771; N = 120, adj. R² = 0.170. Its footnote calls the adjacent numbers t statistics and ** means p < 0.05; no usable SE for this total comparison is explicitly supplied (p. 9). Indirect effect via cognitive diversity: b = −0.283, SE = 0.091, 95% CI [−0.513, −0.134]; serial indirect effect via negative socio-emotional reactions and cognitive diversity: b = −0.061, SE = 0.029, 95% CI [−0.148, −0.021] (p. 9, Sections 4.2-4.3.1; p. 10, Table 2). Originality-only robustness: serial indirect effect b = −0.105, SE = 0.050, 95% CI [−0.248, −0.036]; cognitive diversity-to-originality path b = 4.619, SE = 1.346, p < 0.01 (p. 11, Section 4.4.2). No arm means or total/direct AI contrast for originality are printed. Regression signs are copied unchanged: unequal access is the reference group, so negative full-access coefficients favor unequal access. SE/CI availability here refers to mediation results, not the main total contrast.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Section 4.1; p. 9, Figure 4A, Table 1 Model (1), and Sections 4.2-4.3.1; p. 10, Table 2; pp. 10-11, Section 4.4.2; p. 12, Figure 6; p. 6, Section 3.4.1 (reference coding); p. 11, Table 3 (arm N values are teams).

contrasts.reported: Unequal access M = 5.654, SD = 0.080; no access M = 4.981, SD = 0.094; t = −5.103, p < 0.01 (p. 8, Section 4.1). Table 1, Model (1), prints No access to AI b = −0.6730***, adjacent column headed SD = −5.1990; N = 120, adj. R² = 0.170. Its footnote describes t statistics and *** means p < 0.01 (p. 9). Numeric signs are as printed, with unequal access as regression reference. This compares the later unequal-access task with the common earlier no-AI phase; no-AI observations also include teams later given full access. It is not a randomized AI-versus-no-AI comparison or an after-AI outcome.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Section 4.1; p. 9, Figure 4A and Table 1 Model (1); p. 6, Sections 3-3.3 and 3.4.1; p. 7, Figure 3.

outcomes.name: Cognitive diversity between the two teammates’ spoken contributions
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Audio-recorded team discussions were transcribed and manually corrected. Each member’s utterances across the whole discussion were concatenated, encoded with the Universal Sentence Encoder, and normalized to unit length. Cosine distance between the two members’ vectors measures cognitive diversity (p. 7, Section 3.4.3). The scored outputs are spoken contributions by different people within a team, not final press releases across teams. The reported PROCESS model N = 60 is used for n_units (p. 8, Section 4), with teams as the analytical units; the paper does not reconcile this with the repeated no-AI and AI phases. Models that replace task quality by originality or change the interaction-concentration measure remain robustness analyses of this same diversity measure (pp. 11-12, Sections 4.4.2-4.4.3 and Figures 6-7).

contrasts.reported: Unequal access M = 0.631, SD = 0.011; full access M = 0.510, SD = 0.018; t = 5.938, p < 0.01. Mediation-model direct path for full access relative to the unequal-access reference: b = −0.107, SE = 0.025, p < 0.01 (p. 9, Section 4.2). SD labels are copied from the prose; the Figure 4 caption describes its error bars as ±1 standard error of the mean. Larger cosine distance means greater diversity, and the negative coefficient is full minus unequal access, not a negative effect of unequal access.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Section 4.2 and Figure 4C; p. 10, Figure 5; p. 7, Section 3.4.3; p. 8, Section 4 (model N); p. 11, Table 3 (arm N values are teams).

contrasts.reported: Unequal access M = 0.631, SD = 0.011; no access M = 0.609, SD = 0.012; t = −1.299, p = 0.197. Mediation-model direct path for no access relative to the unequal-access reference: b = −0.017, SE = 0.020, p > 0.1 (p. 9, Section 4.2). The no-AI observations come from the earlier common baseline, including teams later assigned full access; this is not randomized AI-versus-no-AI evidence. The paper reports independent-sample t-tests despite the repeated-phase design (pp. 8-9, Section 4.2).
contrasts.locator: pp. 8-9, Section 4.2; p. 9, Figure 4C; p. 10, Figure 5; p. 6, Sections 3-3.3; p. 7, Figure 3.

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine distance d(W_i, W_j) = 1 − cos(W_i, W_j) between normalized vectors; larger values indicate greater cognitive dissimilarity (p. 7, Section 3.4.3).
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Universal Sentence Encoder (USE), TensorFlow Hub; no model version or specific module URL is given (p. 7, Section 3.4.3).
diversity_detail.computed_over: The two members of each team: each person’s utterances are concatenated across the entire discussion, and the two resulting vectors are compared. This is within-team, between-person semantic distance; it is not all pairs of submitted press releases within an experimental arm (p. 7, Section 3.4.3).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Independent-sample t-tests across conditions (pp. 8-9, Section 4.2) and PROCESS/path-analysis coefficients with SEs (pp. 8-10, Section 4 and Figure 5). Figure 4 error bars are labeled ±1 SEM, whereas the prose calls the accompanying dispersions SDs. The PDF does not explain how repeated observations of the same team are handled for the no-AI comparisons; no participant- or team-clustered SE procedure is stated.
diversity_detail.notes: Retained as across_people because the computed measure compares contributions from different people, but its scope is the two collaborating teammates, not homogenization across independent teams’ final products. No similarity-to-diversity sign reversal was performed: the measure is already a distance. Negative regression coefficients use unequal access as the reference (p. 6, Section 3.4.1).

company_involvement.description: No company involvement in conducting or funding the research is reported. Both authors have a university affiliation; the authors report no financial support and no commercial or financial relationships constituting a conflict. Moonshot is identified only as the Kimi developer.
company_involvement.locator: p. 1, author affiliation; p. 6, Sections 3 and 3.2; p. 14, Funding and Conflict of interest.

eligibility.reason: The treatment-phase comparison randomly assigns teams to unequal versus full generative-AI access, so it qualifies as ai_design (p. 6, Sections 3 and 3.2). The study reports 120 people in 60 two-person teams, with both analyzed team groups represented in Table 3, exceeding the people threshold (pp. 5-6, Sections 3 and 3.1; p. 11, Table 3). Blinded experts score the submitted press releases on task quality including originality, and originality is also used as the sole task-quality indicator in robustness analysis (pp. 6-7, Section 3.4.2.1; pp. 10-11, Section 4.4.2). Core eligibility applies to unequal versus full access; the fixed-order, different-prompt no-AI comparisons do not meet the random-assignment criterion. The transcription-based diversity measure is distinguished from diversity across final products.

one_line_finding: Unequal AI access yielded higher task-quality grades than full access (5.654 versus 5.250; t = 2.881, p < 0.01) and greater semantic distance between teammates’ spoken contributions (0.631 versus 0.510; t = 5.938, p < 0.01; pp. 8-9, Sections 4.1-4.2).
open_questions: Are the dispersions labeled SD in Sections 4.1-4.2 actually SDs or SEMs? Figure 4 says its error bars are ±1 SEM; the labels cannot be reconciled from the PDF (pp. 8-9).

Table 1 labels adjacent columns SD but prints negative values and describes t statistics in its footnote. The main total-effect SEs are not explicitly available; clarify the table before effect-size extraction (p. 9).

How were repeated no-AI and AI observations handled? Table 1 reports N = 120, the PROCESS models report N = 60, and Section 4.2 uses independent-sample t-tests. Confirm analytical rows and team dependence before pooling precision (pp. 8-11).

Obtain the external supplement to verify the exact scoring rubric and whether any additional outcome statistics are supplied; only its contents as described by the main text could be confirmed (pp. 6-7 and 14).

Should within-team semantic distance between spoken contributions be included in the same diversity display as between-person or between-team final-output homogenization? Preserve this distinction (p. 7, Section 3.4.3).
The candidate record lists DOI 10.1002/pra2.1437 as another version. The saved PDF does not establish whether it shares this sample; do not assume independent participants or confirmed overlap.
notes: Read the complete markdown conversion, including references, in six contiguous chunks; inspected all PDF figures and tables and checked recorded statistics against the relevant PDF pages. The saved PDF ends with references and contains no appendix or supplement. Outcome inventory: Figure 4 and Table 1 report task quality, completion time, and cognitive diversity; Figures 5-7 and Table 2 additionally report positive and negative socio-emotional reactions and concentrated questioning/answering as mediators; Figure 6 and Section 4.4.2 substitute originality for task quality; Table 3 gives baseline measures and covariates (pp. 8-12). The two outcome entries retain task quality including its originality-only robustness variant, and diversity. Completion time measures efficiency rather than a scored creative output and is omitted from the outcome entries; the interaction frequencies/ratios measure communication processes rather than creativity or diversity and are also omitted. Baseline self-ranked team creativity and problem-solving are covariates, not creative-output scores (p. 8, Section 3.4.5). The original and difference-score versions of the interaction mediators do not create additional creativity outcomes. No distinct outcome results for writing quality or content quality are printed. Table 3 is explicitly a control-phase baseline comparison (p. 10, Section 4.4.1), not the AI-phase result. No after_ai outcome is reported: no-AI production preceded AI use. The 120 participants form one study and are not counted again for the second task; per-arm numeric people counts are left null because the paper prints arm counts only as teams. No shared participants or reanalysis of another paper is stated; adaptation of Noy and Zhang’s task does not establish sample reuse (p. 6, Section 3.3). No public data or code URL is given: the data statement says raw data will be made available by the authors (p. 14). All statistics retain their printed signs and labels; no effect sizes or missing standard errors were computed. Retrieval of the named supplement URL and DOI URL with User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1 both failed with WinError 10013; no supplement contents beyond the main-text descriptions were assumed.
